item.title: What I’m thankful for, literarily.
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: personal reflection, literary appreciation

What I’m thankful for, literarily.

– Listening to a poem while doing my little stretches. The Library of Congress and Poetry Archive collections, to be specific.

– And I’m thankful in advance to the programmer who builds me a little widget or website that streams a random poem from these archives.

– The new Marlon James. I’m late to the party, but damn.

– Finding something cool in a pile of books someone is giving away.

– The major book awards no longer being afraid of support for Palestine, and Paradiso 17 and Huna winning NBAs.

– A really good pen. I’ve had two instances recently where I had a small bookstore coupon that I spent on luxe pens. Highly recommend treating yourself to a fine writing instrument.

– Funny novels with funny first person narrators.

– The tide continuing to turn against AI. I’m thankful we may see AI’s high water mark very soon.

– Getting to interview Adam Peterson for the release of his story collection.

– Booksellers, who are in the middle of their most hectic season. I’m thankful for everyone who treats them reasonably this time of year.

– Peanuts, a Perfect Snack For Reading.

– Librarians, who are always in the middle of hectic season.

– Flaming Hydra, and especially Luke O’Neil’s recent New England Week which I’m revisiting as I pack up to go to Boston for the holiday.

– Connecting with a stranger over a book, especially that thing where someone points at your book from a distance, and you close it and hold up the cover, and they give you a thumbs up. Really good stuff.

– Small presses, and all the cool and weird things they’re taking a chance on.

– Marilynne Robinson. Her middle name is Summers, but she’s an autumn writer.

– My sweet seven month old showing preferences for books. And I also chew on the books that I like, so I’m thankful that he inherited that trait from me.

– Trying to explain Gene Wolfe’s deal to someone for the first time.

– A small book you can read in an afternoon. Also having an afternoon free to read.

– Olga Ravn’s gift guide, which includes Ibuprofen and haunted dolls.

– Reading an author who is really going for it and trying something new. I appreciate someone taking a risk, regardless of the outcome. (Usually.)

– A friend asking for a book recommendation, and then actually reading your recommendation, and then telling you they liked your recommendation. No better feeling in the world.

James Folta

James Folta is a staff writer at Lit Hub and the managing editor of Points in Case. He co-writes the weekly Newsletter of Humorous Writing. More at www.jamesfolta.com, or you can reach me at jfolta@lithub.com.

item.title: Mourning is a Tide in “Flee”
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original narrative, exploration of themes

Set in the foggy aftermath of the pandemic, the debut novel Flee by Tim Raymond introduces readers to an alternate world dissolved by the rapid spread of Novel Aquatica, a virus with the capability of transforming infected individuals into beluga whales. The plot follows former ESL instructor Jensen Fisher, a person with autism in his late thirties, as he is forced out of the comfort of his apartment in South Korea and into the responsibility of caring for one of his students, Min-kyoung, after she loses her mother to the virus. Simultaneously urgent, funny, and heartbreakingly reflective in its memories, Flee is about the everchanging landscape of loss and how to rediscover peace within oneself.

The plot strings together elements of autofiction, climate fiction, and something akin to a post-apocalyptic survival journal, all while maintaining a feeling of reminiscence, love, and mourning. Raymond identifies as an autistic, nonbinary writer based in South Korea, and they sincerely reflect aspects of their identity into our narrator, such as the concept of social masking, stims, and thought patterns associated with what a person with autism can experience. The story opens with a hark to Herman Melville as Jensen states his name and the intent for why he sets out to tell his journey. As Jensen and Min-kyoung quickly realize they cannot stay in Jensen’s apartment, the two set out with Jensen’s cat Ori on a roaming quest to find a means to keep living.

Memory and forms of coping are peppered throughout the novel. A love for videogames helps both Jensen and Min-kyoung navigate the turmoil of a world plunged into demise. Jensen references characters from games like Zelda: Breath of the Wild and Hades as the two search for food in abandoned malls or consider routes of survival along the mountainside. As the group encounters survivors, Jensen flashes to experiences with family members he has lost connection with or moments with his wife Yoon, who passed away prior to the events of the novel. Interacting with strangers throughout their travel has Jensen recounting how he was sometimes misperceived in his autism with talking to people prior to the spread of the virus. And yet, Raymond excels in showing the beauty and creativity and resourcefulness abundant in people with autism. In one leg of the journey, both Jensen and Min-kyoung talk to and care for a woman who is infected and mutating into a whale. As the woman loses speech and terrestrial mobility, Min-kyoung reassures her and helps her move to a nearby river.

The organic nature by which the memories ebb and flow feels akin to our reality, wherein the thoughts of the past are sometimes used to inform our present or, alternatively, how memory can intrude, harm, or distract us entirely from goals we set out to achieve. Often, chapters begin with a recollection of a time before the pandemic or find themselves slipping in between Jensen and Min-kyoung’s conversations. Mostly effective, the direction was temporarily lost and disoriented a few times until Jensen is pulled back to the present through means of the plot.

Romanticization of Korean culture is touched upon, but could have been fleshed out more in Jensen’s reflections of his time in the country. On rare occasions, Jensen may generalize or discuss elements of the Korean language in a manner that feels glamourized. At one point in which the author Raymond counters this, Min-kyoung cautiously points out to Jensen how a cluster of survivors intentionally chose foreign representatives to lead the two around their encampment. She believes the survivors do this to convince Jensen, the perceived adult and foreigner in the situation, of the encampment’s safety. Less attuned to the nuances within Korean culture, Jensen is brought to this observation by his former student.

Like memory, themes of isolation, familial dynamics, and placelessness shift and come in and out of focus across Flee. What does home mean when someone finds themselves in a lifestyle of constant relocation? How does grief both connect and separate us from one another? As people form relationships or pull away from our lives, how do our siblings and children and lovers move with them? Raymond’s storytelling—whether it be of sailors sharing their travels, people surviving and describing illness, or immortal videogame characters trudging through the afterlife—can help represent alternate or marginalized perspectives and reveal how what appears to be a stable ground of self-understanding may actually be an unfathomable sea of learning and relearning.

FICTION

by Tim Raymond

Button Poetry

Published on November 24, 2026

Danny Rivera (he/they) is a Chicago-based reader, writer, and reference librarian at both Truman College and DePaul University. They completed their Masters in Library Science through the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign in 2025. When not working in the stacks or assisting students with research, their head always rolls to queer horror, fantasy, and science fiction. They live with their partner, Ry, and their two black cats, Pan and Grim. They are currently working on a dark little fairytale novel.

Source: Chicago Review of Books | Published: 2026-11-25 11:00 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

item.title: The Fire-Hose Style of Journalism: A Dirge for Salon
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: historical context, analysis of journalism

Document

In the dying days of 1995, I was a freelance journalist in Portland, Oregon, who spent most of my time seated at a rickety particle-board desk, a gift from my father-in-law. The desk was covered in faux-walnut laminate and swayed from side to side as I wrote. I had already finished my main financial gusher for that year, a history book for fifth graders, and I needed more work.

In this respect I was no different than any freelancer in literary history. In fact, the technology involved in my trade, and the speed at which it functioned—its industrial metabolism—had hardly changed in the preceding century. Of course, I had a computer. But it hardly seemed to be much more than a glorified typewriter. And of course I had an email account, courtesy of the nerd Valhalla known as CompuServe. But the business of freelance journalism was still built largely around stuffing wads of paper into envelopes and sending them to editors, who would then transform the contents into other wads of paper: newspapers, magazines, books. The product, whatever you thought of it, was palpable.

Into this cozy Victorian setting came an online publication called Salon. It had been launched that same fall by a crew of ex-staffers from the San Francisco Examiner, traditional journalists trying to break the mold. I don’t remember which Salon editor contacted me in the first place. I do remember reading the website in my chilly little office, steadying the stupid desk with one leg and feeling an almost metaphysical puzzlement. Salon wasn’t some programmer’s hobby, whipped up in creaky old COBOL. It looked like a magazine, with zippy graphics and respectable fonts. The prose was smart, stylish, and amusingly contrarian.

All of this made a kind of sense to me. What was tricky was that it was free. That first afternoon, I printed out one of the articles, about The Beatles Anthology, which was just then airing on TV. I suppose I was turning back the technological clock—transubstantiating the product back into paper. Reading Salon gratis made me feel as if I were doing something furtive, as though I were a shoplifter, but it represented a kind of post-Gutenberg freedom.

Over the next year, I would write many pieces for Salon. I started out with book reviews that were assigned to me by Dwight Garner. (He had previously edited a few things of mine at Vogue, in terms of ethos the absolute inverse of Salon and, eventually, in terms of finances too.) Dwight sent me books by the bushel, or so it felt. I wrote very short pieces for him very quickly; they appeared online almost immediately. This, for the journalist, was unprecedented and nearly beggared belief. No more waiting for your piece to come out, pacing the equivalent of a widow’s walk. Sometimes I was even instructed to send the piece straight to the copy editor so we could cut a few more minutes out of the process.

Speediness of reflexes was part of the value proposition for Salon. Within months, the “smart tabloid,” as its founder David Talbot called it, was posting daily rather than weekly. In this way it inaugurated a fire-hose style of journalism that would in time become universal. The new norm was not waiting, not allowing stories to lose their heat in the cooling saucer of classic media.

Salon’s politics were similarly nontraditional: left-leaning, libertarian-adjacent (as per its Bay Area digs), but without an obvious party line. It doubtless helped that the magazine was not a subsidiary of a larger corporation, which was the case with Slate (part of Microsoft) and the earlier, cruder Mr. Showbiz (part of Starwave, a short-lived multimedia platform founded by Microsoft’s Paul Allen). Yes, Salon’s seed funding had come from Apple—a mingy $60,000—followed by a more substantial disbursement to the tune of $2 million from the Adobe cofounder John Warnock and various other investors. But it was an independent entity, unconstrained by the need to tiptoe around the feelings of a corporate proprietor.

In any case, I wasn’t writing about politics. I was writing about culture: the magazine’s strong suit. From books I branched into music—I believe it was Joyce Millman, Salon’s television critic, who assigned me pieces about Prince, Los Lobos, Bill Frisell, Cassandra Wilson. These were my enthusiasms, not the sort of dutiful, indiscriminate coverage that a film-critic friend of mine once likened to servicing a vending machine. I was allowed to venture further still when I pitched a piece about Martin Scorsese’s use of music. (The Casino soundtrack, I wrote, struck me as what the director might listen to “if he were shipwrecked with nothing but a polyester suit and a bank of slot machines.”)

It wasn’t long before I was writing short personal essays. I wrote one about being hoaxed by the founder of the Church of Kurt Cobain, which turned out to be nonexistent, although certainly plausible in the drizzling, grunge-friendly atmosphere of Portland. I wrote another about becoming addicted to All My Children during a serious family health crisis in the midst of which I found myself strangely inspired by the surreal resiliency of the characters, who never died unless their respective actor’s contracts with the show expired. I’m not making any extreme claims for these pieces. They were written at the madcap pace dictated by Salon and sandwiched between other freelance explorations—of dental malocclusion or aluminum smelting, say. For me, though, they still evoke the adrenaline feel of the period, the wild sense of participating in something new and transformative.…

Source: The Paris Review | Published: 2026-11-25 13:00 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

item.title: The Green Elf
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original short story, exploration of relationships

When Kyle finally told Lucy the truth, he hid under the covers. They’d been on the sofa, his head in her lap as she touched his hair, coaxing him, telling him he could just say what was bothering him, whatever it was. No sooner had he told her than he sprang to his feet, ran to the bedroom, and pulled the duvet over his head. She coaxed him again, robotically now, to come out.

“Of course you’re not bad,” her voice replied to his muffled question.

He’d been working up to this, she realized, for weeks or months. Like on that night, walking home through Union Square, when he’d told her there were things he wanted to do—things he’d hoped he would no longer want now that he was with her, but that he found he still wanted. She remembered then, as she watched the sidewalk glitter beneath her steps the way sidewalks do in New York under the streetlamps, how he’d told her early in their relationship that she’d miraculously eliminated his snoring. Spooning her, he believed, had been the cure. Now his cavernous snores filled their room each night, his great, heavy arm pinning her in place. She often found herself awake under its weight, scootching her body an inch at a time, attempting to shift positions without waking him. In those moments, the world seemed to gape at her with its darkness.

She hadn’t worried on that night walking home. She’d felt special. She knew she was exceptional—the only girl, out of so many, he’d ever given a key to. From the first time they met, she’d felt chosen by him. His compliments, the way he cleared his schedule for her, the dinners and theater tickets. It was she who’d hesitated. She’d found his eyes beady, his skin sallow and cold, his mouth in a permanent downward curl. But the dating history he relayed made it clear hers was the minority opinion, and he was tall and had two Ivy Leagues on his resumé and his jokes were cutting. One morning lying in bed, six weeks after she’d graduated college and three weeks after she’d first messaged him (she liked the app where only women could initiate), he asked if that night at Sean’s, he could introduce her as his girlfriend. She felt a twinge of revulsion, of panic. She said not yet. No. She left his apartment. But later that day, he called her while she was in the park with her friend Jesse. Was it okay, he asked, if he slept with his ex-girlfriend?

“What?” she said.

“She’s coming over to pick up her stuff. Since you said you don’t want to be my girlfriend, is it okay if I sleep with her?”

She was angry, furious. At the end of the call, she agreed to be his girlfriend.

After his confession that day on the couch, the childlike refrain stuck. You’re good, she’d tell him when he grew insecure. She’d pet his forearm from elbow to wrist, going with the grain of his hair, soothing, until he stopped bucking and turned soft and pliable, like a willing child. She liked exercising this ability, a talent she might not otherwise have discovered.

That phrase was the only trace of what he’d told her that was ever mentioned between them, a sort of oblique reference; beyond that, the matter was set aside. He was not active, and so she agreed not to tell anyone.

“Even your therapist,” he said after coming out from below the duvet.

“Okay,” she replied, but she told her therapist anyway.

Afterwards, she panicked that Kyle would find out she’d told, but of course he didn’t. She was comforted by her therapist’s response that consenting adults were consenting adults. As time passed, she nearly forgot about it. There was the time she opened her old laptop, which had been in a corner of their apartment collecting dust for over a year, and several windows opened automatically that made her worry. She was proud she’d closed the browser without reading, but she asked him about it. Were they pop-ups?

“Yeah,” he said, “must’ve been.” She figured he’d just been watching porn on it. And then there was that smudge on his cheek, the one he said was his colleague Tanya’s mauve lipstick. When they went to dinner at Tanya and her husband’s, Lucy noted with relief that her lipstick was in fact mauve.

Of course, now and then—rarely at first, more often as their first couple years went by—he made a joke about it. The week she moved in, after they painted a misguided accent wall that would lurk in her peripheral vision for years like a square, mustard bruise, he asked her to try it just once, to celebrate the occasion. She said it’s not funny, and he said no, it is, and that night when he slept, she pushed his arm off her without caring if he woke, which he didn’t. Around his birthday or the holidays—Christmas was the worst time for him, despite his professed love of it and his insistence that they perform every tradition, tree trimming parties and mulled wine and old cartoons—he kidded about what he wanted for his present. She’d purse her lips and turn away, and he’d touch and pinch her and pretend they were flirting, and she’d think about how long and ugly his face could be, how his smile could be so joyless.

The first time she did it was on his birthday in their third year together. Thirty, still far in the future for Lucy, seemed like the age of an adult to her. He brought it up while they were having dinner at his favorite restaurant, Squid. In the months leading up to this, she’d felt his growing frustration. It was a darkness that lapped at the edges of his voice, his hulking shoulders, sometimes overflowing and swallowing them both. One night he crumbled to the floor, drunk and naked, like an oversized fetus with a vortex of despair swirling around him, and she stood over him, unmoving, perched on the precipice of a black hole. Afterwards, her memory of the occasion was hazy, but still it left its mark on her, like a thumbprint in a newly opened container of Play-Doh.

But on his birthday, at the restaurant, he approached her like a lawyer with his deal points outlined, ready to negotiate yet optimistic about his prospects.…

Source: The Rumpus | Published: 2026-11-25 13:05 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

item.description:

Why it is here: collection of poems, variety of themes

How to Choose Grief

Make a little ghost

out of your knees

and the sheet.

Tell the doctor, No,

I would not like to

get dressed before

we speak. Sometimes

babies slip like light

through the leaf

of their skin,

and you’re told

it’s likely, could be

guaranteed. Ask no one

how many cold bowls

of strawberries or

books have to be

consumed before

it’s considered

a good life. If you could

line up her days like feet

you might not make it

to the bird feeder, or

your mailbox at the end

of the street. Imagine

feet dangling

above the white tiles

in the kitchen, a wet

mouth sounding out

words, each broken

syllable beautiful

as blue egg shells

in the grass.

Whatever happens

is what is colored

by the wind.

A tea bag’s worth of ashes,

a pack of unwashed

bee-print bibs.

Sing to that feeling

of something

in your belly—petals

unfurling in a vase

despite the flower

being cut.

***

Stealing My Mother’s Lingerie

Like peeling the reflection

of trees off a lake or lifting

the pink from peonies—

but my boyfriend asked for

a photo and my stretched-out

skivvies wouldn’t do.

The see-through pink

made my hips hyperbolic,

my breasts tits. I stood

in front of the full-length

and snapped picture

after picture for two

hours for a wow. After

the seams parted like lips

in the wash (I didn’t know

it needed to be soaked

in the sink) I slid

the spaghetti Mom made

over it in the trash.

I knew she knew what I’d done.

Still, she brought home soft

pretzels after her appointment—

God it felt good letting

the hot salt scrape my tongue.

There’s nothing I want more

than to be forgiven.

***

Sweetness

Before the first peony

splatter of sauce

is scrubbed

from her onesie,

the doctor is talking

about lifespan, what

the heart can and

can’t endure over

multiple surgeries.

Her first scar

before her first sleep.

My husband steals

cookies for me

from the waiting room

because complimentary

surely can’t cover this

toteful of shortbread

and sweetness

is something

that needs to be

pilfered these days.

At home I sew

a felt heart,

not anatomical,

with little flowers

and French knots.

I sew another

and another;

in our bedroom

is a basket full

of hearts. The apple

tree next door drops

its sweet ornaments

for the rabbits,

or the dirt—

I can’t stop making

things I don’t know

if she’ll ever hold.

***

More Wing

after Red Bird, 1964, Agnes Martin

Your hand in my hair

too is a bird

unboundaried by

shape

a bird bleeding

into sky like rosé

into a tablecloth

what’s more wing

than your sigh

slicing the air

like light I return

to this

foreplay of a pink

so pale

you almost

miss it

when we kiss

in the kitchen

the dish gloves drip

like rain off petals

the almost-birds

of our mouths

my back

makes the banana

magnet release

its menu

I swear

we make

nothingness

blush

Source: The Rumpus | Published: 2026-11-25 14:16 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

item.title: I Share a Closet With His Emotional Baggage
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: short story, exploration of relationships

Lit Mags

I Share a Closet With His Emotional Baggage

"How to Live Rent-Free in Someone's Head," flash fiction by Kate Francia

I Share a Closet With His Emotional Baggage

This article is free to read. So is every article Electric Literature publishes. No limits, no paywalls—now or ever. Support from readers like you makes that possible.

We need to raise $60,000 to start off 2027 strong. Donate now to our end of year fundraiser to help ensure the future of free, accessible literature for all.

—————

How to Live Rent-Free in Someone’s Head

I took Jacob up on his offer. Yes, it was soon-ish to make such a big move—just a month and change since we got together officially—but we’d known each other for longer, and I felt like it could be something real. My lease was up. He said there was space. My sister was being dramatic about how I would lose my identity and become nothing more than the idea of me in his mind. But honestly, the bigger thing I was worried about was Marnie.

I was not made aware that Marnie would be there. That first day, I walked in and found her stretched out on the futon, painting her toenails green.

“Hi!” she said. “You must be Jill. Jacob’s told me so much about you.”

Obviously I knew who Marnie was. I was probably the world’s living expert on Marnie after all the time I spent listening to Jacob cry about her, back before he and I got together.

“Is that all you brought?” She pointed to my garbage bag. I twisted my hands through the pull strings. Most of my things were in storage in my sister’s basement. “It’s just temporary,” I said. “Until we can get a real place.” Then Marnie offered to help me unpack, which, no.

I had been looking forward to that part, the taking things out of the bag and putting them in places, that new-drawer feeling. But there was no drawer. Jacob had said he would clear one out for me, but every drawer I opened was full of random stuff, clothes and socks and stacks of receipts but also a conch shell, a box full of plastic straws, a sewing kit, a saxophone—and of course I started to wonder if all of this stuff was Jacob’s or if some of it was Marnie’s.

It was like a regular apartment. Except it had no windows and too many doors, most of them locked, and the unlocked ones opening into closets packed with junk that fell on you if you opened them. It’ll be just like having our own place, he’d said, and it sort of was, except most of the time he wasn’t there. It smelled like him, and I remembered all the times I had lain awake in my old apartment wishing I could be there. But at odd moments I’d be brushing my teeth or sweeping the floor and Marnie would walk by, crunching her way through a giant bag of crackers. Also I was pretty sure she was using my shampoo.

“I’m not,” said Marnie. “You’re using my shampoo.”

I pulled a chunk of my hair to my nose and sniffed it.

You might wonder why I’d bother washing my hair there. But I always thought Jacob might come in at any second. When he was there, there were things like a kitchen table and a TV and a bed, things that made it feel like home. He almost never came in during the day, though, even though to me the whole benefit of our situation was that theoretically he could check in anytime.

Hey babe what time are you—

“He’s not coming,” said Marnie. “It’s game night.” She pulled out her guitar and started singing the same song, over and over and over.

When he was there, though, it was so great. One night he came in full of all this energy and curled his arms around me, burrowed his head into my shoulder. ”I don’t know how you put up with this place. God, what a mess.” He clomped around, pulling open all the closets and opening boxes of stuff. He dumped things out on the futon: a winter coat, a fondue maker with two little silver sticks. He wanted to make space for me, to give me the kind of place I deserved.

“Check these out!” He spread baseball cards on the floor. “I haven’t looked at these in ages. I bet some of them are worth a lot.” He formed stacks, then shuffled them all together and formed different stacks.

“He’s not going to clean it up, you know,” said Marnie, hours later. She sat cross-legged in a nest of flannel green plaid camping blankets. I couldn’t see the futon or any of the furniture. Jacob was gone for the night.

“Maybe I could just start with some of the big things.” I pulled an empty box and started putting things in it. Old sporting equipment, school papers, a guitar. I wrote “high school” on a label. Marnie watched from her nest.

“You could help,” I said.

“Why would I do that?”

“Maybe because you live here too?”

“You should leave it. It’s his crap.” She sounded like my sister.

“I’m his girlfriend. A good girlfriend.” I tried to pull another box down and sent a cascade of stuff tumbling down over the box I’d just packed. Marnie snorted.

“What are you even doing here?” I said. “No one wants you.”

“Ouch. I’m devastated.” She took a long slurp of Diet Coke.

I made a lot of progress over the next few days. Or, I think they were days. I didn’t like to admit it, but if Jacob forgot to check in after work, it was hard to tell one day from another. But it was nice to have a project, a purpose. And that weekend, Jacob and I had plans to spend some quality time together, just us. I straightened a stack of books, fluffed a bunch of silk flowers I’d found scattered among some old vintage dresses.

“Sorry I’m late, babe. I don’t know why you put up with me.”

I jumped up and wrapped my arms around him. The way he smelled, the laundry soap and the buzz of his voice against my chest. It felt real. We were going to spend the evening just watching bad TV in a clean room and maybe we could talk about the future, about us. “Hey,” he said, “where are my baseball cards?”

He tore through box after box. “Why would you do this? I didn’t say you could touch my stuff!”

“I was trying to help.” I picked at a strand of my hair, the ends split and split again. “Marnie left it really messy.”
